words.gloss_range: coordinating connector that carries the denial catalog across the ayah boundary; not a fresh independent sentence opener here
words.prose: {{ar:وَ}} ({{tr:wa-}}) opens 50:13 as a connector, so the reader has to carry the denial predicate from 50:12 into the new names rather than read a fresh sentence. Its repeated short onset also starts a three-beat pattern: each entry is added side by side, with the omitted verb making the catalog compact while the cadence keeps each name distinct.

topics.headline: connector carries the prior denial predicate
topics.reader_payoff: The reader notices that 50:13 is grammatically dependent on 50:12, so the list continues one denial predication instead of starting over.
topics.reason: The local ayah has coordinated names but no new predicate, and attachment evidence marks the denial verb from 50:12 as understood for the names in 50:13.

topics.headline: repeated connector makes compact accumulation audible
topics.reader_payoff: The reader hears the catalog as measured accumulation: short repeated connectors add separate cases while one omitted act of denial governs them all.
topics.reason: The first connector begins the local recurrence later repeated before the second and third entries, so its payoff is rhythmic addition as well as syntactic linkage.

words.gloss_range: proper name for the people of Aad as a coordinated subject under the carried denial predicate; root-return pressure is associative, not a replacement for the proper-name sense
words.root_gloss_range: broad root range includes return, repetition, habitual recurrence, return-place, and the accepted proper-name branch; the local surface selects the proper-name branch while allowing recurrence imagery to color the catalog
words.prose: {{ar:عَادٌۭ}} ({{tr:ʿādun}}) is the first content name after the boundary, but its nominative role depends on the denial verb already supplied in 50:12. Its tanwīn does not make it indefinite; it marks a fully declined proper name, unlike the foreign diptote that follows. Its first slot also reopens a familiar destruction-catalog pairing with Pharaoh rather than naming an isolated people. The root {{ar:ع و د}} ({{tr:ʿ-w-d}}) keeps return and habituated recurrence in the background, so the name works as a remembered people and as a warning that denial patterns come back.

topics.headline: nominative name depends on the prior verb
topics.reader_payoff: The reader sees the first name as a subject of the inherited denial verb, not as a free-floating historical label.
topics.reason: The word is nominative and coordinated in a verbless ayah, while attachment evidence explicitly projects the prior denial predicate into 50:13.

topics.headline: tanwīn marks declension, not indefiniteness
topics.reader_payoff: The reader does not mistake the tanwīn for indefiniteness; the form is still a definite proper name with a distinct recited ending.
topics.reason: QAC marks the word as a nominative proper noun with tanwīn, allowing the form contrast with the following no-tanwīn foreign title.

topics.headline: return-root colors the proper name as recurrence
topics.reader_payoff: The reader hears the named people inside a root field of return and habit, making the catalog feel like recurring denial rather than mere archival listing.
topics.reason: V4 keeps the proper-name branch available for the local noun, so the name remains Aad; the return and habituation branches supply controlled associative pressure, including a broader root echo with restoration language at 85:13.

topics.headline: first post-boundary name reopens a known warning catalog
topics.reader_payoff: The reader notices that Aad is not only one example; its first position after the boundary reopens the warning series and links to familiar destruction-pair patterns.
topics.reason: Distributional evidence places Aad in repeated warning-catalog settings, and the local position makes it the pivot from the prior list into the 50:13 triad.

words.gloss_range: middle coordinating connector that adds Pharaoh as a parallel entry under the same inherited predicate
words.prose: The middle {{ar:وَ}} ({{tr:wa-}}) keeps Pharaoh from becoming an apposition to Aad or a fresh clause. It gives the singular ruler the same grammatical rank as the surrounding peoples, and its short repeated sound divides the catalog into equal beats.

topics.headline: middle connector separates and equalizes Pharaoh
topics.reader_payoff: The reader notices that Pharaoh is added as an equal catalog subject, not as an explanation of Aad or as a new sentence.
topics.reason: The particle coordinates the second named entry under the inherited denial predicate and blocks an appositional reading between the neighboring names.

topics.headline: repeated short onset resets the list rhythm
topics.reader_payoff: The reader hears the second connector as a refrain beat that keeps each catalog item individually registered.
topics.reason: The same short connector recurs before the middle entry and prepares the third occurrence, making coordination audible as patterned accumulation.

words.gloss_range: foreign proper royal title, nominative under the carried denial predicate; Arabic f-r-ʿ resonance is associative sound-field pressure, not the local lexical root
words.prose: {{ar:فِرْعَوْنُ}} ({{tr:firʿawnu}}) stands in the middle as a foreign royal title: definite without tanwīn, yet nominative under the same carried denial predicate. The title compresses palace and ruler into one archetype of power, while Arabic f-r-ʿ resonance adds height and branching-overreach as sound-field pressure. Structurally, one ruler is placed between two collective entries, so political singularity is made equivalent to communal denial.

topics.headline: foreign title is definite and no-tanwīn
topics.reader_payoff: The reader notices the center entry as a marked foreign royal title, not a tanwīn-bearing native-style proper noun like Aad or Lūṭ.
topics.reason: QAC marks the word as a foreign proper noun and diptote with no tanwīn while still nominative and definite by title status.

topics.headline: middle name shares the carried predicate
topics.reader_payoff: The reader sees Pharaoh governed by the same prior denial predicate, despite the ayah supplying no local verb.
topics.reason: The word is nominative and conjoined to the other entries, so the inherited verb from 50:12 governs this singular ruler along with the collective names.

topics.headline: great-house title becomes ruler archetype
topics.reader_payoff: The reader catches how a foreign palace-title can name a ruler while also resonating in Arabic with height, branching, and overreach.
topics.reason: The local word has no QAC root and remains the foreign title Pharaoh; the f-r-ʿ material is therefore kept as controlled Arabic resonance and metonymic title history, not as an asserted local derivation.

topics.headline: single ruler pivots between collectives
topics.reader_payoff: The reader notices that one tyrant is placed at the same catalog level as whole peoples, making him a compressed archetype rather than a narrated episode.
topics.reason: The middle slot places a singular royal figure between collective entries, and the supplied occurrence evidence supports his standalone use as a destruction-catalog type.

words.gloss_range: final coordinating connector that opens the construct phrase as the third equal catalog entry
words.prose: The final {{ar:وَ}} ({{tr:wa-}}) does not make the last phrase an explanatory tail after Pharaoh. It opens the longest member of the triad as a third coordinated subject, completing the connector refrain while shifting the catalog from direct names to relational naming.

topics.headline: final connector opens a new coordinated phrase
topics.reader_payoff: The reader sees the final phrase as a full third catalog member, not as a subordinate explanation attached to Pharaoh.
topics.reason: The particle coordinates the construct phrase with the earlier names under the inherited predicate and separates it from the preceding proper title.

topics.headline: third connector completes the refrain before relational naming
topics.reader_payoff: The reader hears a clipped reset before the longest and most relational catalog entry, so the close feels both parallel and expanded.
topics.reason: The third connector completes the repeated wa-frame and marks a referent-type shift from a royal name into a construct phrase.

words.gloss_range: plural construct head meaning communal fellows or brothers of Lūṭ; locally relational and communal rather than biological siblinghood
words.root_gloss_range: root family centers brotherhood, companionship, shared belonging, and kinship-like solidarity; local form selects communal brotherhood in a construct phrase
words.prose: {{ar:إِخْوَٰنُ}} ({{tr:ikhwānu}}) changes the final entry from direct naming into a construct relationship. The plural head is nominative under the carried denial predicate, but it is grammatically incomplete until Lūṭ supplies the genitive anchor; the group is identified through relation to the prophet. The root {{ar:أ خ و}} ({{tr:ʾ-kh-w}}) gives that relation the feel of communal belonging and obligation, not biological siblinghood, so the denial catalog turns brotherhood language into culpable solidarity. The wording also reverses the prophet-brother formula known from 26:161: here the community bears the brotherhood label.

topics.headline: construct head makes the group identifiable through Lūṭ
topics.reader_payoff: The reader notices that the final group is not directly named; its identity is grammatically opened by brotherhood and completed by Lūṭ.
topics.reason: The word is the construct head governing the following proper name, and the phrase is a coordinated nominative subject under the inherited denial predicate.

topics.headline: communal brotherhood becomes culpable solidarity
topics.reader_payoff: The reader sees that the people are framed as communal fellows bound by obligation around Lūṭ, making their denial a relational failure.
topics.reason: The local plural and construct syntax support communal belonging rather than biological siblings, while the denial frame reverses the positive social force into indictment.

topics.headline: plural form foregrounds a network, not one name
topics.reader_payoff: The reader notices the final entry as a network of fellows shaped by a specific brotherhood plural, rather than a singular name or a generic people label.
topics.reason: The word is a plural noun in construct state, and the row evidence distinguishes the communal plural from narrower biological sibling forms while preserving its recited long-vowel shape.

topics.headline: prophet-brother formula is reversed
topics.reader_payoff: The reader catches a formulaic echo: instead of Lūṭ being called their brother as in 26:161, the community is named as brothers associated with Lūṭ.
topics.reason: The supplied co-occurrence and formula evidence includes 26:161 and related prophet-brother patterns at 26:106, 26:124, and 26:142; 50:13 changes the direction of the relationship.

topics.headline: relational noun slows the final catalog member
topics.reader_payoff: The reader feels the close lengthen: the final entry remains parallel in cadence but becomes more mediated through construct syntax.
topics.reason: The fronted relational noun shares the nominative cadence with the previous entry but delays completion until the following genitive name.

words.gloss_range: proper name in genitive construct position completing the phrase brothers of Lūṭ; supplied l-w-ṭ imagery is associative and does not replace the proper-name reference
words.prose: {{ar:لُوطٍۢ}} ({{tr:lūṭin}}) completes the final construct phrase as a genitive proper name, so the group becomes identifiable only when this name lands. Its tanwīn marks a fully declined proper name and gives the ayah a nasalized final closure. The supplied l-w-ṭ adhesion and denial fields add controlled pressure: the community is grammatically attached to Lūṭ while the inherited denial frame makes that attachment morally tense. As the last word, the name also compresses wider Lūṭ scenes, including the stone-rain destruction (54:34), and helps complete a broader triad of varied judgments with Aad by wind (51:41) and Pharaoh by drowning (20:78).

topics.headline: genitive name completes the construct
topics.reader_payoff: The reader notices that Lūṭ is not merely appended; his name completes the grammatical dependency that identifies the final group.
topics.reason: Attachment evidence marks the word as the genitive complement of the construct head, making it the dependency-completer of the final phrase.

topics.headline: tanwīn and emphatic close mark the landing
topics.reader_payoff: The reader hears the final name land with a marked genitive tanwīn closure, distinct from the no-tanwīn middle title.
topics.reason: The proper name is genitive with tanwīn, so its ending both signals construct dependency and supplies the ayah's final recited closure.

topics.headline: adhesion and denial imagery press on the proper name
topics.reader_payoff: The reader feels a tension between attachment to Lūṭ and denial of the message: the grammar binds the community to him while the carried predicate indicts them.
topics.reason: The surface remains the proper name Lūṭ with no QAC root assignment; the l-w-ṭ adhesion and denial material is retained only as root-family pressure triggered by the construct attachment and inherited denial frame.

topics.headline: final name compresses wider Lūṭ destruction scenes
topics.reader_payoff: The reader notices that the closing name can summon the wider people-of-Lūṭ destruction register, including the stone-rain scene at 54:34, without retelling it.
topics.reason: The supplied references make Lūṭ a compact narrative recall point, and the triad evidence compares Aad by wind (51:41), Pharaoh by drowning (20:78), and Lūṭ by stone rain (54:34).

topics.headline: last word lands the second wave of the catalog
topics.reader_payoff: The reader feels the ayah close on the denied messenger's name after passing through a relational phrase, making the boundary a rhythmic hinge inside one catalog.
topics.reason: The name is final in the ayah and completes the second wave of bare-name accumulation after 50:12's verbal proposition.

baseline_models.focus_anchor: The coordinated nominal chain `Ad, Pharaoh, and the brothers of Lot.
baseline_models.mechanism: The proper-name branch fixes `Ad as a tribe, while the brotherhood branch marks the last entry by relationship. Repeated coordination places a tribe, a ruler-name, and an affiliated group on one corporate roster.

activation_trace.role: The tribe-name branch fixes `Ad as a historical corporate label in the coordinated roster.
Brotherhood and kinship supply the relational label by which Lot's associated group enters the roster.

changed_reading.before: Three names or labels are merely juxtaposed.
changed_reading.after: The ayah is a deliberately mixed corporate roster whose entries can be represented by tribe, political center, or relational group.

baseline_models.focus_anchor: The plural relational noun إخوان attached to Lot.
baseline_models.mechanism: The inventory allows both kinship and a tether or bond. The phrase can therefore name a brother-like affiliation organized around Lot, without requiring that only biological siblinghood be in view.

activation_trace.role: The kinship branch supplies the ordinary brotherhood relation and its extension toward friendship.
The tether branch recasts brotherhood functionally as a bond that holds an affiliated group together.

changed_reading.before: The phrase points only to Lot's literal brothers.
changed_reading.after: The phrase may designate people held together by a brother-like social bond around Lot.

baseline_models.mechanism: The proper-name branch remains primary, but the same focus inventory also supplies return after departure. The tribal name can carry a latent recurrence or return echo without ceasing to be a name.

context_deltas.mechanism: The whole-surah sequence moves from disputed return from dust, through emergence from dead land, to the returning person and final destination. That sustained motion reactivates the focus inventory's return branch inside the name `Ad, making the cataloged past participate in the surah's forward return arc.

activation_trace.role: The tribe branch preserves `Ad as the literal roster entry rather than replacing the name with an abstraction.

structural_cues: The activators span 50:3, 50:11, 50:32, and 50:43, so the effect belongs to the whole-surah package rather than only the adjacent catalog.
context_deltas.reader_inference: The packet supplies several return, emergence, and destination branches; I infer that their repetition reactivates the same branch under the proper name `Ad. The live alternative is that `Ad remains semantically opaque and the recurrence is only formal.

changed_reading.before: The ayah interrupts resurrection discourse with a detached list of past names.
changed_reading.after: The `Ad entry remains historical but also becomes a lexical hinge joining past recurrence to the surah's promised return.

context_deltas.mechanism: The flanking ayat label groups as a people and as companions; the focus substitutes tribe-name, ruler-name, and brothers. The closing totalizer then assigns every entry the same rejection of messengers and the same binding threat. The focus line is therefore the middle panel of a taxonomy of corporate affiliation, not a self-contained name list.

context_deltas.reader_inference: The packet supplies alternating group labels and a final totalizer, rejection, and threat; I let that closure back-propagate over the focus line and infer a taxonomy of affiliation. A live alternative is a simpler additive list with no special force in the label variation.

changed_reading.after: 50:13 is the center of a three-ayah social taxonomy whose diverse corporate forms are equalized by one rejection and one consequence.

The later judgment scene decomposes collective solidarity into an accountable self plus its attached relations, so إخوان no longer offers anonymous shelter inside a group.

context_deltas.reader_inference: The packet supplies the scale shift from named collectivities to each self with attached figures; I infer that this shift functionally dissolves collective anonymity. context_deltas.reader_inference: The packet supplies shared split-root branches of counting, preparation, and scheduled recurrence; I infer that they can organize the names as installments in a timed pattern. surprising_valid_outliers.containment: This is surprising because it transfers a material cord and the act of binding into a social noun. It remains anchored in the focus inventory's explicit tether branch and in exact whole-surah cord and pairing branches; downstream prose should present it only as a possible structural resonance, never as a replacement lexical meaning for إخوان or as a claim of literal restraint.
surprising_valid_outliers.focus_anchor: The الآخية or tether branch supplied for focus word إخوان.

activation_trace.role: Ordinary brotherhood keeps the outlier attached to the actual relational noun.
A tether or fastening supplies the focus-side image of social attachment.

changed_reading.before: Brothers are simply members of a named kin category.
changed_reading.after: Exploratorily, the brothers form a tethered affiliation network whose very bonds make it a coherent accountable unit.

strongest_changes: The closure in 50:14 turns the focus into the middle panel of a three-ayah taxonomy of corporate affiliation and supplies its shared act and consequence.
The whole-surah return, emergence, returner, and destination sequence reactivates a latent return branch under the proper name `Ad.
The later movement to each self, driver, witness, and companion revises collective brotherhood into a bond whose members remain individually exposed.
summary.what_was_special: The focus is extremely short and largely nominal, so the strongest activation came from whole-surah sequence and from the packet's split mappings: a proper name stayed literal while acquiring return, habit, and counted-recurrence resonances, and a kin term acquired both social and material bond mechanics.
remaining_uncertainties: Whether a proper ethnonym such as `Ad can sustain root-level return resonance beyond formal wordplay.
Whether إخوان here favors literal kinship, broad affiliation, or both.
Whether the non-dominant mappings to habit and counting are discourse activations or only lexicographic accidents.

reader_a.activated_readings_md:
1. **A proper name sits inside the surah's return vocabulary.** `ع و د:B012` licenses Aad as a proper name, while `ع و د:B001` supplies returning and doing again. The list structurally repeats earlier rejecters; I infer a controlled resonance in which Aad is both correctly a name and part of a recurrent pattern. The ayah reads as historical enumeration and patterned return without conflating the branches.
2. **Brotherhood marks a binding social unit.** `ء خ و:B001` supplies kinship and `ء خ و:B002` a tethering bond. In proximity to group rejection, I infer that “brothers of Lot” foregrounds solidarity capable of binding a community into a shared stance. The designation is socially functional, not merely genealogical.
reader_a.retrospective_surprises_md: 50:36's `قَرْن` and 50:44's universal gathering corrected the local bonds here: kinship and named collectives organize people temporarily, but they do not exempt any generation from the larger return-and-gathering sequence.

reader_a.activated_readings_md:
1. **The proper name ʿĀd overlaid by return.** `ع و د B012` secures the fixed form as the proper name ʿĀd, while dormant `ع و د B001–B002` supply returning after departure and the place or time of return. The name stands between *khurūj* from dead land (50:11) and “new creation” (50:15), with paired receivers appearing in 50:17. The packet supplies that placement; I infer a word-level return resonance without replacing the proper-name reading. ʿĀd consequently participates in the surah’s return mechanism even while remaining a historical name.

2. **Brotherhood as an accountability tether.** `ء خ و B001` supplies brotherhood and association, while `ء خ و B002` supplies a tethering bond or protected obligation. Within the window, the human is described through the cord of the jugular in 50:16 and flanked by two receivers in 50:17. Those material relations are supplied; I infer that the “brothers of Lot” are a socially bound unit whose association carries shared exposure to consequence. *Ikhwān* reads as more than loose companionship: it is a relation that holds members together when acts become reportable.
reader_a.retrospective_surprises_md: 50:15’s new creation unexpectedly activated return inside the proper name ʿĀd without displacing `ع و د B012`. Then 50:16’s cord and 50:17’s paired receivers made the tether image in `ء خ و B002` functional: social association appears as a bond that remains accountable.

scoping.note: SCOPED, NOT ABSENT. The surah-scope fallback inventory covers every root in the surah; it is narrowed here to roots this ayah can justify -- roots occurring in this ayah (all their branches kept, unconditionally, because Layer 2 selects nothing) plus roots explicitly cited by channel material anchored here (only the cited branches kept, enough to resolve the citation). A root listed in dropped_roots is a deliberate scoping decision, not a missing source.

v12_reader_responses.note: Per-ayah focus-run reader responses are retired from the default commentary workflow. Use regular reader walks, plus/minus-5 reader walks, and cross-run publication findings for corpus-wide reader-derived evidence.

v12_cross_run_publication.note: Compact final cross-run findings for this ayah, reconciled upstream from regular and plus/minus-5 reader runs; use as a coverage/priority check, not as replacement prose.
